candidates.topic: The Gaviotas Experiment — Rainforest Grown From Scratch
candidates.teaser: A group of scientists turned a barren, lifeless plain into a thriving rainforest — and they did it in just 20 years.
candidates.video_title: They Grew a Rainforest From Nothing in 20 Years
candidates.video_description: In the Colombian savanna, a small eco-village called Gaviotas did what experts said was impossible — they restored an ancient rainforest on dead soil. The trees came back, then the animals, then the rain itself. Science has no full explanation for how it spread so fast.
candidates.script: Scientists said nothing could grow there — the soil was dead, the land completely barren. But in 1971, a small Colombian village called Gaviotas planted a single species of pine on the savanna. Within 20 years, something impossible happened. Ancient rainforest species that had been gone for centuries started returning on their own — plants, insects, jaguars. The pines hadn't grown a forest. They had woken one up. So what exactly was sleeping beneath that soil?

candidates.topic: The Taos Hum Twin — Kokomo Hum Indiana
candidates.teaser: Hundreds of people in one small American town heard a sound that drove them to madness — but microphones recorded nothing.
candidates.video_title: A Sound Only Some People Can Hear Is Destroying Lives
candidates.video_description: In Kokomo, Indiana, residents reported a relentless low-frequency hum that caused nosebleeds, dizziness, and chronic pain. Scientists investigated for years. They found two industrial sources — but turning them off changed nothing. Some people still hear it today.
candidates.script: In 2000, people across Kokomo, Indiana started going insane from a sound no recording device could capture. Nosebleeds, joint pain, crippling headaches — all from a hum only some residents could hear. Scientists spent years investigating. They found two industrial sources and shut them down. The hum kept going. Roughly 2 percent of humans can perceive frequencies others physically cannot. But here's what no one has answered: why does it only get louder at night?

candidates.topic: The Patagonian Toothfish Rename — Marketing Changed Everything
candidates.teaser: One of the most popular fish on the planet was completely unsellable — until someone simply changed its name.
candidates.video_title: They Renamed This Fish and Made Millions Overnight
candidates.video_description: The Patagonian toothfish was considered worthless and impossible to sell for decades. In 1977, a fish wholesaler renamed it 'Chilean sea bass' — a fish that isn't a bass and isn't always from Chile. It became one of the most expensive items on restaurant menus worldwide within a decade.
candidates.script: This fish sat rotting in markets for decades because nobody would buy it. The name alone killed every sale — Patagonian toothfish. In 1977, a Los Angeles fish wholesaler renamed it Chilean sea bass. It's not a bass. It's not always from Chile. Didn't matter. Within ten years it was on the menus of the world's finest restaurants at forty dollars a plate. The fish hadn't changed at all. So what does that tell you about every other choice you think you're making freely?

candidates.topic: The Last Breath of Julius Caesar — Carbon in Every Room
candidates.teaser: With every single breath you take right now, you are almost certainly inhaling atoms that were once inside Julius Caesar.
candidates.video_title: You're Breathing Julius Caesar Right Now
candidates.video_description: Every breath contains roughly 10 sextillion air molecules. Caesar's dying breath has had over 2,000 years to mix into Earth's atmosphere. The math is unambiguous — statistically, at least one atom from that breath is in your lungs at this very moment. And not just Caesar's.
candidates.script: Right now, in your lungs, there are atoms that were inside Julius Caesar when he was stabbed 23 times in 44 BC. This isn't a metaphor — it's atmospheric chemistry. Each breath you take holds around 10 sextillion molecules. Caesar's last exhale has had over 2,000 years to distribute evenly across Earth's atmosphere. The math says at least one of those atoms is inside you right now. And not just Caesar — every person who ever lived.

candidates.topic: The Ursula Burns Xerox Story — Intern to CEO
candidates.teaser: She told the CEO of Xerox he was wrong — to his face, in a room full of executives. Two decades later, she replaced him.
candidates.video_title: She Told the CEO He Was Wrong — Then Became Him
candidates.video_description: In 1989, Ursula Burns, a young Black engineer at Xerox, openly challenged a senior executive during a meeting. Instead of being fired, she was noticed, mentored, and placed on a leadership track. In 2009, she became CEO of Xerox — the first Black woman to lead a Fortune 500 company in US history.
candidates.script: In 1989, a young Black engineer at Xerox stood up in a meeting and told a senior vice president he was flat wrong — in front of everyone. Most people would have been quietly removed. Instead, Xerox's CEO heard about it and personally requested to mentor her. Twenty years later, Ursula Burns sat in that CEO's chair herself, becoming the first Black woman to lead a Fortune 500 company in American history. The question is: how many people stayed silent in that same room and went nowhere?
